name: Amritsar
tagline: The spiritual home of Sikhism: a gold-domed temple shimmering on a sacred pool, a kitchen that feeds tens of thousands a day and the food of the Punjab.
highlight: The Golden Temple at dawn, when the gold reflects in the still water and the hymns begin.
shortDescription: The Punjabi city of the Harmandir Sahib, or Golden Temple, with its free community kitchen, the Jallianwala Bagh memorial, the Partition Museum and the daily border ceremony at Wagah.
metaDescription: An Amritsar travel guide: the Golden Temple, the langar, Jallianwala Bagh, the Partition Museum, Wagah-Attari border ceremony, Punjabi food, visiting etiquette and a two-day plan.
nearestAirport: Sri Guru Ram Dass Jee International (ATQ), about 30 minutes
knownFor: The Golden Temple, langar, Punjabi food, Jallianwala Bagh, the Wagah border
goodFor: Spiritual experience, food, history, a change from the tourist trail

image.alt: The gold-covered Harmandir Sahib temple reflected in the sacred pool at Amritsar

intro: Amritsar was founded in 1577 by Guru Ram Das, the fourth Sikh guru, around a sacred pool, and it has been the spiritual centre of Sikhism ever since. The Harmandir Sahib, known to visitors as the Golden Temple, sits in the middle of the pool, and its gold-plated upper floors were added in the early 19th century under Maharaja Ranjit Singh. The Guru Granth Sahib, the Sikh holy scripture, is read there day and night.

The Golden Temple is unusual among great religious sites in how open it is. People of every faith and none are welcome, entry is free, and the community kitchen, or langar, serves free vegetarian meals to tens of thousands of people every day, prepared and served by volunteers. Visiting is one of the most welcoming spiritual experiences in India.

Amritsar also has darker layers of history. The Jallianwala Bagh, where British troops killed hundreds of unarmed civilians in 1919, is a short walk from the temple, and the Partition Museum records the upheaval of 1947, when the Punjab was split between India and Pakistan and millions were displaced. The city is also a centre for Punjabi food, with kulchas, lassi and tandoori dishes.

whyVisit.intro: Amritsar is one of India's most moving and welcoming places, and less touristy than the Golden Triangle.

points.title: The Golden Temple
points.text: A serene, glowing temple on water, with an atmosphere of devotion and hospitality.

points.title: The langar
points.text: One of the world's largest free kitchens, open to all, where visitors can eat and help.

points.title: History that matters
points.text: Jallianwala Bagh and the Partition Museum tell important stories of modern South Asia.

points.title: Punjabi food
points.text: Amritsari kulcha, chole, lassi and fish, in its home region.

points.title: The Wagah border ceremony
points.text: A theatrical daily flag-lowering at the India-Pakistan border.

attractionsIntro: The Golden Temple is the centre of the city, with the other sights within walking distance or a short ride.

attractions.name: The Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple)

image.alt: The Golden Temple and its sacred pool in Amritsar

attractions.text: The holiest Sikh shrine, in the centre of the Amrit Sarovar pool, reached by a causeway. Visitors walk around the pool, and can queue to enter the temple itself. The complex is at its most beautiful at dawn and at night.
attractions.tip: Cover your head, remove shoes, wash your feet and avoid tobacco and alcohol.

attractions.name: The Guru Ka Langar
attractions.text: The community kitchen, where volunteers cook and serve simple vegetarian meals of dal, roti and rice to tens of thousands of people every day, eaten sitting on the floor.
attractions.tip: Accept the meal with both hands, and consider helping to wash dishes.

attractions.name: The Akal Takht

image.file: File:Akal Takht and Harmandir Sahib, Amritsar, Punjab, India.jpg
image.alt: The Akal Takht building beside the Golden Temple complex in Amritsar

attractions.text: The seat of temporal authority in Sikhism, facing the Golden Temple, damaged in 1984 and rebuilt.
attractions.tip: Ask a volunteer to explain the history.

attractions.name: Jallianwala Bagh

image.alt: The memorial gardens at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar

attractions.text: A walled garden where, on 13 April 1919, British troops fired on a crowd, killing hundreds of civilians. A memorial and a preserved well mark the site, and bullet marks remain on some walls.

attractions.name: The Partition Museum
attractions.text: A museum in the old town hall that records the 1947 Partition of India through personal stories, letters and objects.

attractions.name: The Wagah–Attari border ceremony

image.alt: The border gates and stands at the Attari–Wagah ceremony ground

attractions.text: A daily ceremony at the border with Pakistan, about 30 km from Amritsar, where soldiers on both sides lower the flags with marching and stamping. It has been scaled back at times when tensions have risen.
attractions.tip: Check whether the ceremony is running and in what form.

thingsToDoIntro: Amritsar rewards those who take their time at the temple and eat well.

thingsToDo.title: Visit the Golden Temple at dawn and at night
thingsToDo.text: The mood changes through the day, and both early morning and evening are memorable.
thingsToDo.tip: Stay for the palki sahib procession at night, if it suits your schedule.

thingsToDo.title: Eat in the langar
thingsToDo.text: Sit on the floor with pilgrims and share a simple meal.
thingsToDo.tip: Take only what you can eat, and do not waste food.

thingsToDo.title: Try Amritsari kulcha
thingsToDo.text: Stuffed leavened bread baked in a tandoor, served with chole and butter.

thingsToDo.title: Walk the old city
thingsToDo.text: The lanes around the temple are full of shops selling phulkari embroidery, juttis (shoes) and sweets.

thingsToDo.title: Visit Gobindgarh Fort
thingsToDo.text: An 18th-century fort turned heritage attraction, with shows and exhibits.

thingsToDo.title: Watch the border ceremony
thingsToDo.text: A boisterous show of patriotism, whose atmosphere is lively.

foodIntro: Amritsar's food is robust Punjabi cooking, with wheat, dairy and tandoor at its centre.

foods.name: Amritsari kulcha
foods.text: A stuffed flatbread of potato or paneer, baked in a clay oven, served with chole and a knob of butter.
foods.whereToTry: Famous kulcha shops in the old city.

foods.name: Chole bhature
foods.text: Spiced chickpeas with puffy fried bread.

foods.name: Amritsari fish
foods.text: Fish fillets in a spiced gram flour batter, deep fried until crisp.

foods.name: Lassi
foods.text: A thick, sweet yoghurt drink in a large glass, topped with cream.
foods.whereToTry: Ahuja Milk Bhandar and other shops.

foods.name: Tandoori chicken and butter chicken
foods.text: Punjabi classics, cooked in the tandoor.

accommodation.intro: Staying near the Golden Temple is convenient, and many pilgrim guesthouses take foreigners.

areas.name: Near the Golden Temple
areas.text: Guesthouses and hotels in the old city.

areas.name: Ranjit Avenue and Mall Road
areas.text: Mid-range and luxury hotels, in the newer parts.

gettingThere.intro: Amritsar is in the far north-west of India, near the Pakistan border.

options.text: About 5 to 6 hours on the Shatabdi express, or overnight on other trains.
Direct flights from Delhi and other Indian cities, and some international routes.
options.detail: The airport is about 30 minutes from the city.

options.text: About 450 km from Delhi, taking 7 to 9 hours.

gettingAround.intro: The old city and the temple are best on foot, and rickshaws and cabs cover the rest.

options.text: The temple, the Bagh and the old city are within walking distance.
To Wagah, and to the airport.

bestTime.headline: October–March
bestTime.summary: Amritsar has hot summers and cold winters, with fog from December to January.

seasons.text: Cool and clear, though fog can delay travel. Nights are cold.
Warm and pleasant. Vaisakhi in April is a major Sikh festival.

bestTime.avoid: May and June. Gurpurab celebrations in November are wonderful but crowded.

itinerary.title: Two days in Amritsar
itinerary.intro: The temple and history on the first day, and food, the border and the old city on the second.

days.title: The Golden Temple and history
days.morning: The Golden Temple at dawn, and langar.
days.afternoon: Jallianwala Bagh and the Partition Museum.

days.title: Food and the border
days.morning: Kulcha for breakfast, and the old city.

tipsIntro: A few points of etiquette make the visit smoother.
tips: Cover your head at the temple. Scarves are available at the entrance.
Remove your shoes, and wash your feet in the shallow channel.
Do not bring tobacco, alcohol or drugs into the complex.
Dress modestly, and behave with respect.
Follow local guidance about photography, and do not take photos of people at prayer without permission.
Check the status of the Wagah ceremony before making plans.
Consider a donation to the langar.

faq.q: Can non-Sikhs visit the Golden Temple?
faq.a: Yes. It welcomes people of all faiths, and entry is free.
Modest clothes, with your head covered and shoes removed.

faq.q: How many days do you need in Amritsar?
faq.a: Two days, or one long day if you are short of time.

faq.q: Is the Wagah border ceremony open?
faq.a: It has been open to visitors in normal times, but it has been scaled back or suspended during periods of tension, so check locally.
It is generally safe and friendly, and used to visitors.
The langar is vegetarian. The city also has excellent non-vegetarian dishes.
